title: Narada sings, and God comes
hookLine: a song that is nothing but names, and the boy who saw God once and spent his life singing to call him back
carry: sing his names and he comes, as if called

lines: NAMES LIKE LANTERNS ON A WIRE.
cards: Govinda jaya jaya, Gopala jaya jaya. Radha Ramana Hari, Govinda jaya jaya. On paper it barely looks like a song.

No story, no request, hardly a rhyme. Just names, and the word jaya, victory, hung between them like lanterns on a wire. A kirtan can ride that line up to a fast, clapping peak and then let it fall back to a whisper.
Someone hearing it for the first time might ask where the meaning is. It's in the names themselves, and in the story of a boy who became a singing sage.

teach.b: Each name in the song is a small portrait of Krishna. Govinda and Gopala belong to his cowherd years in Vraja. Hari is a name of Vishnu, and devotees honor Krishna as one with Vishnu.
Radha Ramana is the one who delights Radha. Now a story about why anyone would sing them. In the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Narada remembers an earlier life.
He was a serving woman's little son, who waited on wandering holy men one rainy season and listened as they sang of Hari.
Later, left alone, he walked into a forest, sat under a tree and thought of the Lord, and for a moment the Lord appeared in his heart. Then it was gone.
A voice told him he wouldn't see that form again in this life; the glimpse was given so he would long for more. So the boy did the one thing left.
He went through the world singing the names. And Narada says that ever since, when he sings of the Lord's deeds, the Lord appears quickly in his heart, as if called. The Gita backs him.

teach.h: THE GITA: ALWAYS SINGING MY GLORY.
teach.b: In chapter nine Krishna describes the great-souled ones, in paraphrase: always singing my glory, striving, firm in their vows, they worship me.

teach.h: SING, AND HE COMES AS IF CALLED.
teach.b: The word for singing his glory is kirtayantah, and you can hear kirtan in it. That's the Hindu teaching under every kirtan, nama-sankirtan: the names aren't decoration.
For devotees, singing them is a way of calling God, and being heard.

how: Krishna devotees sing Govinda jaya jaya and similar strings of names at kirtans and in homes, often speeding up toward a clapping peak and slowing again to a hush.

o: a story-song that tells Krishna's life in order
a list of names memorized for a scripture exam
songs known by heart, here a string of Krishna's names

games.q: the names in the song — tap the pairs.
p: saw the Lord once, then sang to call him

s: the Gita never mentions singing God's glory
in chapter nine Krishna describes the great-souled as always singing his glory: kirtayantah.
in the Bhagavata, Narada says the Lord appears in his heart when he sings
he says when he sings of the Lord's deeds, the Lord appears quickly, as if called.
a kirtan song needs a story to have meaning
Govinda jaya jaya is only names, and each name carries a story with it.

games.q: you're Narada as a boy. you saw the Lord in your heart for one moment, and a voice says not that way again in this life. what do you do?
o: go through the world singing his names, calling.
sit under the same tree and wait forever.
games.why: Narada sang the names, and says the Lord now appears in his heart quickly, as if called. that's the hope inside every kirtan.

practice: Bring to mind a few names you've called out in your life, a parent, a friend, a child, a pet at the door, and notice how each one carries a whole person, and how your voice changes for each.
If you pray, take one name of God from your own tradition and say it silently, slowly, the way you'd call someone you hoped would come; if not, rest with the feeling of calling and being called.

wordCard.voice: Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: Govinda jaya jaya, a string of Krishna's names, sung the way Narada sang them, as a call.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: kirtayantah, singing the glory, the Gita's word in chapter nine; you can hear kirtan in it.

carryVoice: Your line: sing his names and he comes, as if called. That's Narada's promise. Day nine hundred ninety, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 1.6.33 (Narada: when I sing his deeds, he appears in my heart as if called)
Bhagavata Purana 1.5–1.6 (Narada's earlier life: the serving woman's son, the glimpse in the forest, the voice)
